job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Amira Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Amira, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my Nana in her terraced house in Armley, in Leeds, and my day runs on lists. Up at seven, tea with Nana, then three hours on applications and the careers portal. I did civil engineering, top of my year, with a summer at a surveying firm and another with the council highways team. Afternoons I walk Nana's dog, do her shopping, and meet my friend Beth for a coffee if I can afford it. Five months since graduating and I've had four interviews and no offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's probably the sensible outcome and I'd be glad of it. I'd tell people that the tools help a bit with paperwork, like the site reports I wrote on my internship, and that's all. I use AI now and then to tidy a report, and it saves me twenty minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau means nothing gets better or worse, and right now that's not enough for me. I owe about twenty-nine thousand pounds, there aren't many civil engineering graduate posts around Leeds, and councils keep freezing hiring. So the squeeze carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my lists going. I'd apply to the water company, the rail network, and the big contractors' graduate schemes that reopen in the new year. I'd chase the highways team lead from my internship, who said to stay in touch. And I'd keep helping Nana, who covers my keep and tells me not to worry, which I do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady worry, like a low hum. Not dramatic, but it's there when I wake up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said councils keep freezing hiring. What did you see on the internship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A desk with a retired engineer's name tag still on it, empty for months. The team lead told me they'd lost three people in two years and replaced one. I learned a lot, but I also learned how thinly it's all stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Nana say when you talk about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says, I've survived worse, and gives me a tenner for the bus. I never take more than I need. She worked in a mill and then at a school canteen, and she's proud of the degree, which makes it harder.

I use AI **now and then** to tidy reports, saving twenty minutes.
think: Nothing getting better isn't enough, with **twenty-nine thousand pounds** of debt.
Councils keep **freezing hiring**, so the squeeze carries on.
do: Apply to the **water company**, rail network and contractors' graduate schemes.
Chase my **internship team lead** who said to stay in touch.
Keep helping **Nana** and run my application lists.
feel: **Steady worry**, like a low hum on waking.

fieldNote: Her **internship** gave her first-hand proof of thinly staffed councils.
Receives quiet **support from Nana**, but avoids taking more than she needs.
Organised and **list-driven**, which fits her steady character.

steps.text: Apply to the water company, rail network and contractor schemes
Email the highways team lead from the internship each month
Keep the daily application lists and the job portal checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I've seen already: the report writing, checking and planning get passed to software and the human does the sign-off. I'd tell my friends we need to be the ones who can sign off, not the ones who type. And I'd say that out loud at a careers event.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my entry-level work is partly on that list. Checking drawings, writing site notes, drafting survey summaries. But civil engineering still needs people on site, so I think I'm in a better position than my friends in pure software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get steadier with the tools, since I use them occasionally and I know they'll matter. I'd focus on getting a site engineer role, where I'm out on the ground and the software supports me. I'd also take the chartered engineer route seriously, which means finding an employer who will mentor me. And I'd talk to Nana's neighbour, who's a retired site manager and knows people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. I feel I have some control, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to friends in software who are struggling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my friends in software, keep applying and be willing to take a less glamorous start. I'd also tell my friends to build things people can see. I know it's easy to say when I haven't got an offer either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the search ran on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My coffee dates with Beth, which hurts. Then the gym membership. I'd keep the train pass, because without it I can't get to interviews.

I'd say so at a **careers event**.
think: Part of my **entry-level work** is on that list.
Civil work needs **people on site**, which puts me ahead of friends in pure software.
do: Get **steadier with AI tools**, since they will matter on site.
Aim for a **site engineer** role and the chartered route with a mentor.
Ask Nana's neighbour, a retired **site manager**, for introductions.
feel: **Anxious but steady**, with some sense of control.

fieldNote: Sees **site presence** as her advantage over software friends.
Names her **cuts** precisely: coffee, gym, never the train pass.

steps.text: Practise AI report and drawing tools until I use them daily
Apply for site engineer roles that lead to chartered status
Ask Nana's neighbour, a retired site manager, for introductions
Drop the gym membership and the weekly coffee dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and I'd want proper planning from the government now. Income support, retraining, a say for workers, and companies required to give warning. I'd also say that physical infrastructure still has to be built, and that engineers on site matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be scared. The calculation and design jobs go within two years, and I'd have no savings and a big loan. The one comfort is that building and repairing roads, pipes and bridges is hands-on and probably lasts three years longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job on a construction site or with a contractor, even as a trainee, and get paid. I'd keep my loan payments at the minimum and keep a small cash pot. I'd let the loan company know my situation, and ask Nana whether I can stay until 2030. I'd also ask the highways team lead if I could work as a labourer-technician and learn from the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with a thread of hope from the hands-on part. It feels like holding on to a railing in a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean to be a labourer-technician after four years of study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would sting a bit, but I'd learn the site from the ground up, and I think that knowledge lasts. My granddad worked as a bricklayer. I'd tell myself it's like a family trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is two years different from a longer warning for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't wait for a graduate scheme. I take whatever pays. With longer I could be choosier, and I'd aim for a scheme that trains me properly.

say: It's frightening, and I want **proper planning** now: income support, retraining and early warning.
Physical infrastructure still has to be built, so **site engineers matter**.
think: Design jobs go in two years, and I'd have **no savings** and a big loan.
Hands-on work probably lasts **three years longer**.
do: Take **any site job**, even as a trainee, to start earning.
Keep loan payments at **minimum** and a small cash pot.
Ask Nana to let me **stay until 2030** and ask the team lead about technician work.
feel: **Scared**, with a thread of **hope**, like holding a railing in a storm.
S2.quote: I'd learn the site from the ground up, and I think that knowledge lasts.
fieldNote: Her **hands-on hope** keeps her mood below alarmed.
Connects a **labourer's job** to her granddad's bricklaying, which makes the idea feel less like a step down.
Plans with **Nana's housing** as a safety net.

steps.text: Accept any trainee job on a construction site
Keep loan payments at the minimum and hold a cash pot
Ask Nana to let me stay until 2030
Write to my MP about retraining and early layoff warning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of time if we use it well, and I'd talk about getting ready: new apprenticeships, retraining and public funding for the infrastructure we need anyway. I'd also say that civil engineering is a good field to be in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel cautiously okay. I'd probably get a graduate scheme in the next year, and with a few years of site work I'd be in a good place before the robots arrive. The loan would be shrinking by then. The fear is that jobs I'd be good at are taken by machines faster than I plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply widely and take a scheme with a chartered route. I'd save a hundred and fifty pounds a month, and I'd pick up site skills fast: surveying, setting out, health and safety. I'd learn the project software properly. And I'd try to get Nana a better heating system, since her boiler's old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously calm. It feels like a long journey with a map, so I can plan the stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a chartered route if the world might change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's a real qualification that employers trust, and it doesn't disappear overnight. If I hold it and I'm on site, I'm harder to replace than someone who only did desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most about those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I take the wrong first job, in an office team that gets cut. I'd look at how much of the work is on site before signing anything.

say: Five years is a lot of time if we use it for **apprenticeships** and infrastructure funding.
Civil engineering is a **good field** to be in.
think: I'd probably get a **graduate scheme** within a year and be in a good place before robots.
The risk is that machines take **my kind of job** faster than I plan.
do: Apply widely and take a scheme with a **chartered route**.
Save **hundred and fifty pounds** monthly and learn surveying and setting out.
feel: **Cautiously calm**, like a long journey with a map.
S3.quote: If I hold it and I'm on site, I'm harder to replace than someone who only did desk work.
fieldNote: Wants to repay **Nana's** support with a practical fix.
Mood eases to **uneasy** because her field and a five-year runway help.

steps.text: Take a graduate scheme with a chartered engineer route
Save a hundred and fifty pounds every month
Learn surveying, setting out and the project software on site
Help Nana replace her old boiler

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that a decade is a gift and we shouldn't waste it. I'd say schools and colleges should add practical skills now, and that governments should plan how to share the gains. I'd tell friends to take the time to choose well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel quite settled. I'd get a good job, pay the loan, get chartered, and maybe even be a site manager before anything big happens. Ten years leaves space to adjust, which is more than most people get with big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start in a graduate scheme and spend three years learning the job properly. I'd clear the loan in five or six years, and then maybe a part-time master's in infrastructure management. I'd also volunteer for a school outreach programme, to tell girls about civil engineering. And I'd try to buy a small flat with Beth as a flatmate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. A decade lets me plan something that isn't just surviving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying a flat. How does that sit with the changes ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for something small and cheap, near a train line, so I could move if jobs shift. I wouldn't stretch myself. I'd rather own a bit of something than rent forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, what do you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the time to find the right first job, instead of taking whatever is nearest. I'd go for the chartered route. And I'd stop thinking of the loan as a monster.

say: A decade is **a gift** and we shouldn't waste it.
Schools should add **practical skills** now, and governments should plan to share the gains.
think: I'd feel **quite settled**, with a loan paid and a chartered title in time.
Ten years leaves **space to adjust**, which is more than most people get.
do: Start a **graduate scheme** and learn the job properly for three years.
Clear the loan in **five or six years**, then study part-time.
Volunteer in **school outreach** and buy a small flat near a train line.
feel: **Pretty good**: a decade lets her plan beyond surviving.
S4.quote: A decade lets me plan something that isn't just surviving.
fieldNote: Mood stays **uneasy** because the unknowns still touch the future.
Wants a **flat** near a train line for flexibility.

steps.text: Start a graduate scheme and learn the job for three years
Clear the student loan within six years
Buy a small flat near a train line with a friend

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because the building trades and councils wouldn't have time to change their hiring. What would help is a funded graduate trainee scheme for infrastructure and a pause on loan repayments while jobs are scarce. Also somebody to mentor me through chartered status.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not asking for a miracle. I want one real job and a few years to do it properly, so I can pay Nana back. I think a lot of people my age feel the same.

headlineQuote: I'm not asking for a miracle. I want one real job and a few years to do it properly
portrait: Amira is a **top civil engineering** graduate in Leeds, five months without an offer.
She lives with her Nana in Armley, owes about **twenty-nine thousand pounds**, and runs her search by lists.
She uses AI tools **now and then**, and her internships at a surveying firm and a council shaped her views.
She stays **pragmatic**, blames no one in particular, and sees site work as her protection.
Her mood goes from **anxious** to uneasy as the warning time grows.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because **councils and contractors** wouldn't have time to change their hiring.
whatWouldHelp: A funded **graduate trainee scheme** for infrastructure and a pause on loan repayments.
